name: Epic teaching (the Mahābhārata's Sāṃkhya-Yoga and Mokṣadharma milieu)
regions: northern India — the epics' settings: Kurukṣetra, Hāstinapura, Indraprastha, Mithilā (Videha), Naimiṣa forest, Badarī, Ayodhyā

tradition.text: the Kurukṣetra war and Vyāsa's composition at the junction of the Dvāpara and Kali yugas (Kali traditionally from 3102 BCE); the Rāmāyaṇa in the earlier Tretā yuga

scholarly.text: the epic teaching layers c. 4th c. BCE – 4th c. CE

transmissions_received.what: the imperishable self and Brahman, the hierarchy of senses, mind and intellect, the paths after death, and whole verses
the sacrificial frame (yajña) and the wheel of sacrifice, reinterpreted inwardly
transmissions_received.evidence: BhG 3.9–16; 4.24–33; Anugītā 14.20–24 (the inner sacrifice of the senses)

transmissions_received.what: the enumeration of principles and the discrimination of puruṣa from prakṛti, in Kapila's line
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition-account: Pañcaśikha, 'Āsuri's first disciple', teaches Janadeva Janaka (MBh 12.211.6–18); Kapila named as proclaimer of Sāṃkhya (12.337.60)

transmissions_given.what: the Bhagavad Gītā as the smṛti-prasthāna commented on by every Vedānta school
pre-classical Sāṃkhya enumerations (24/25/26 principles) — on the scholarly account, precursors of Īśvarakṛṣṇa's system
epic yoga vocabulary: dhāraṇā, the five faults of yoga, yoga-power (yogabala), the first dhyāna with vitarka and vicāra
cosmology of the ages and dissolution, lists of the Lord's manifestations, dharma teaching
Rājadharma, Āpaddharma and the Anuśāsana's teaching on gifts, fasts and funerary offerings

distinctive_positions: Action is unavoidable for the embodied; what binds is attachment to the fruit, not action itself (BhG 3.5, 2.47, 18.11).
Several disciplines — knowledge (sāṃkhya), disciplined action (yoga), meditation and devotion — lead to one goal; 'one who sees Sāṃkhya and Yoga as one, sees' (BhG 3.3, 5.4–5, 13.24–25).
The self in the body is unborn, eternal, not slain when the body is slain (BhG 2.12–30).
Prakṛti with its three guṇas is the agent of all action; the puruṣa experiences and witnesses (BhG 3.27, 13.19–22).
The principles are counted as 24 with the puruṣa as 25th, and the Vasiṣṭha–Karāla and Yājñavalkya dialogues add a 26th, the awakened (MBh 12.294–296, 12.306).
Sāṃkhya and Yoga differ in method — Yoga relies on direct perception and argues that without a Lord no one is freed; Sāṃkhya relies on the teaching of the śāstra — yet both are true (MBh 12.289.3–7).
Dharma is subtle: conduct, not birth alone, is said to make a brāhmaṇa (3.177.16, 12.181.10), while the duties of the varṇas are also upheld (BhG 18.41–48; 12.60).
Non-cruelty (ānṛśaṃsya) and non-violence (ahiṃsā) are called the highest dharma (3.297.55; 1.11.12; 13.116), alongside the kṣatriya's duty to fight a righteous war (BhG 2.31–33).
Liberation (brahmanirvāṇa, entering the Lord) can be won in this life by one whose mind rests in equality (BhG 5.19, 5.26, 2.72).

Time (kāla), nature (svabhāva), fate (daiva) and human effort are debated as causes; the Gītā counts daiva as one of five causes of action (18.14) and Bhīṣma teaches that fate does not succeed without effort (13.6.7).
Dharma, artha and kāma are one whole (trivarga) grounded in dharma; 'from dharma come artha and kāma — why is it not practised?' (18.5.49).
summary: The teaching layer of the two Sanskrit epics, above all the Mahābhārata: the Bhagavad Gītā, Bhīṣma's instruction in the Śāntiparvan (Rājadharma, Āpaddharma, Mokṣadharma) and Anuśāsanaparvan, the Anugītā, the Sanatsujātīya, Vidura's counsel, the Yakṣa's questions, Mārkaṇḍeya's discourses, and the dharma teaching of the Rāmāyaṇa. It is not a school with a single doctrine but a milieu in which Upaniṣadic, early Sāṃkhya and Yoga, Vedic ritual, devotional (Bhāgavata) and ascetic ideas are set side by side in dialogues, and which later schools (Vedānta, classical Sāṃkhya and Yoga, the Purāṇas, bhakti traditions) all claim as authority.
notes: Owned by U05. 'Lineage' here names a teaching milieu (a body of texts and dialogues), not an initiatory succession; the tradition itself names chains of transmission within it (BhG 4.1–3; 12.211; 12.336 for the Sātvata dharma).

name: Early Bhāgavata devotion (the Nārāyaṇīya / Sātvata–Ekāntika dharma)
regions: Mathurā and the Śūrasena country; Vidiśā (Besnagar); Rajasthan (Ghosuṇḍī); western Deccan (Nānāghāṭ) — on the scholarly (inscriptional) evidence
Badarī (Nara–Nārāyaṇa's hermitage) and Śvetadvīpa in the tradition's account

tradition.text: the Sātvata dharma was given by Nārāyaṇa at the beginning of the Kṛta age and handed down (MBh 12.336)

scholarly.text: worship of Vāsudeva attested from c. 4th–2nd c. BCE (Pāṇini 4.3.98 'vāsudevaka'; Heliodorus's Garuḍa pillar at Besnagar, late 2nd c. BCE, whose donor calls himself a bhāgavata; the Ghosuṇḍī and Nānāghāṭ inscriptions naming Saṃkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva, c. 1st c. BCE); the Nārāyaṇīya's theology c. 1st c. BCE – 4th c. CE

transmissions_received.what: Sāṃkhya-Yoga categories in which the fourfold form is stated
transmissions_received.evidence: 12.326.100 calls the teaching 'made by Sāṃkhya-yoga, called Pañcarātra'

transmissions_received.what: sacrificial worship reoriented to Nārāyaṇa; the Vedas as part of the teaching
transmissions_received.evidence: Uparicara Vasu's sacrifice (12.323–324); 12.336.76 joins Sāṃkhya-yoga, the Vedāraṇyaka and Pañcarātra

transmissions_given.what: the fourfold form (caturvyūha) and the Sātvata worship of Vāsudeva
lists of the Lord's manifestations (prādurbhāva/avatāra) and Kṛṣṇa devotion (Harivaṃśa, Bhāgavata and Viṣṇu Purāṇas)
devotion to Nārāyaṇa/Kṛṣṇa as the one refuge
the Gītā, Nārāyaṇīya and Viṣṇu Sahasranāma as authorities for Nārāyaṇa's supremacy and surrender

distinctive_positions: Nārāyaṇa-Vāsudeva is the one supreme Lord, the knower of the field whose self is without guṇas (12.326.38).
The fourfold form (caturvyūha): from Vāsudeva comes Saṃkarṣaṇa (the jīva), from him Pradyumna (the mind), from him Aniruddha (the ego), from whom Brahmā arises (12.326.68–69; 12.327.26).
The liberated ascend through the sun into Aniruddha, Pradyumna and Saṃkarṣaṇa and finally Vāsudeva; the one-pointed devotees (ekāntins) enter Vāsudeva directly (12.332.13–18; 12.336.3).
The Lord appears again and again (prādurbhāva) as Varāha, Narasiṃha, Vāmana, Rāma Bhārgava, Rāma Dāśarathi and at Mathurā, and earlier as Haṃsa and Hayaśiras (12.326.71–94); cf. BhG 4.7–8.
Exclusive devotion (ekānta-bhakti), worship according to rule without desire, is the highest dharma, equal to Sāṃkhya-yoga (12.336.4, 12.336.69).
Worship by sacrifice without slaughter (Uparicara Vasu's sacrifice; the dispute over 'aja' as goat or grain, 12.323–324).
Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pañcarātra, the Vedas and Pāśupata are distinct systems, yet Nārāyaṇa is the culmination seen in all (12.337.59–67).
Rudra and Nārāyaṇa are one being made twofold (12.328.24).
The teaching Kṛṣṇa gave Arjuna before the battle is this dharma (12.336.8); taking refuge in the Lord alone frees from all sins (BhG 18.66), even for women, vaiśyas and śūdras (BhG 9.32).
summary: The early devotional religion of Nārāyaṇa-Vāsudeva (Kṛṣṇa) as found in the Nārāyaṇīya of the Mahābhārata, the Bhagavad Gītā's teaching of devotion and surrender, the Harivaṃśa and the Viṣṇu Sahasranāma: exclusive devotion (ekānta-bhakti) to one Lord in a fourfold form, worship without animal sacrifice, and the Lord's repeated appearances to protect dharma. It flows into the Pāñcarātra, the Purāṇic Vaiṣṇavism and the later Vaiṣṇava sampradāyas.
notes: Owned by U05. Scholarly (labeled) observation: the three 'immortal steps' of Heliodorus's inscription — self-restraint, renunciation, heedfulness (dama, cāga, apramāda) — match the triad 'damas tyāgo 'pramādaś ca' at MBh 11.7.19 and 5.43.14.
